## Problem

`config.json:22-31` ships configuration for two backends the binary does not
contain:

```json
  "opencl": { "enabled": false, "cache": true, "loader": null },
  "cuda":   { "enabled": false, "loader": null, "nvml": true },
```

`Dockerfile:29` compiles them out:

```dockerfile
RUN cmake .. -DWITH_OPENCL=OFF -DWITH_CUDA=OFF && make -j"$(nproc)"
```

## Evidence

The built binary reports no GPU backends:

```
$ docker run --rm xmrig:audit /bin/xmrig --version
XMRig 6.22.2
 built on Aug  1 2026 with GCC 15.2.0
 features: 64-bit AES

libuv/1.52.1
OpenSSL/3.5.7
hwloc/2.12.2
```

No OpenCL, no CUDA in the library list. XMRig parses unknown backend blocks
without complaint, so setting `"enabled": true` in either block produces no
error, no warning, and no GPU mining — the key is read into a backend that was
never registered.

The README's tuning table (`README.md:109-113`) documents `randomx.*` and
`cpu.huge-pages` but says nothing about the GPU backends being absent, so
nothing in the repository tells a reader why flipping the switch did nothing.

## Impact

A user who wants GPU mining edits `"opencl": { "enabled": true }` — the config
key exists, the edit looks correct, and the miner starts normally at unchanged
CPU-only hashrate. There is no signal anywhere that the feature is not in this
image. The dead keys actively advertise a capability the artifact does not have.

## Fix

Delete both blocks — they are inert:

```diff
-  "opencl": {
-    "enabled": false,
-    "cache": true,
-    "loader": null
-  },
-  "cuda": {
-    "enabled": false,
-    "loader": null,
-    "nvml": true
-  },
```

and add one row to the README tuning table recording that the image is a
CPU-only build, so the absence is documented rather than merely implied:

| Option | Requires |
| --- | --- |
| `opencl` / `cuda` | not available — the image is built `-DWITH_OPENCL=OFF -DWITH_CUDA=OFF`; rebuild from source to enable GPU mining |

## Resolution
config.json: deleted both dead blocks. README tuning table gained a row recording that the image is a CPU-only build and that adding those blocks back is silently ignored.
title: config.json ships opencl and cuda blocks for backends compiled out of the binary

## Problem

Inside the image, `NOTICE`'s pointer to the MIT licence resolves to the GPL.

`NOTICE:4-6`:

> This repository's own packaging ... is licensed under the MIT License; see
> LICENSE.

`NOTICE:39-43` places itself next to a file of that exact name:

>     Both travel inside the image itself, under /usr/share/licenses/xmrig/ :
>
>         LICENSE    — upstream XMRig GPL-3.0 licence text

`Dockerfile:52-54` ships that layout:

```dockerfile
COPY --from=builder /xmrig/LICENSE /usr/share/licenses/xmrig/LICENSE
COPY --from=builder /xmrig/src/donate.h /usr/share/licenses/xmrig/donate.h
COPY NOTICE /usr/share/licenses/xmrig/NOTICE
```

## Evidence

The repository's own MIT `LICENSE` is never copied into the image — `.dockerignore`
does not exclude it, the Dockerfile simply does not `COPY` it. So in the image:

- `/usr/share/licenses/xmrig/NOTICE` line 6 says "see LICENSE" for MIT terms;
- `/usr/share/licenses/xmrig/LICENSE` is the GNU GPL v3;
- the MIT text is nowhere in the image.

Both statements in NOTICE are individually true, sixteen lines apart, and the
only file named `LICENSE` a reader can reach contradicts the first one.

## Impact

The image is the artifact that travels; NOTICE is the compliance document it
carries, and it misdirects on its own first reference. Someone auditing the
image's licensing — the exact reader this file exists for — follows "see
LICENSE" and finds GPL-3.0 where MIT was claimed, with no MIT text present to
correct the impression. It is a smaller version of the same defect as the `MIT`
value on `org.opencontainers.image.licenses`, and it undercuts the one document
that gets the licensing right.

## Fix

Ship both, named unambiguously:

```diff
-COPY --from=builder /xmrig/LICENSE /usr/share/licenses/xmrig/LICENSE
+COPY --from=builder /xmrig/LICENSE /usr/share/licenses/xmrig/LICENSE.xmrig-GPL-3.0
 COPY --from=builder /xmrig/src/donate.h /usr/share/licenses/xmrig/donate.h
 COPY NOTICE /usr/share/licenses/xmrig/NOTICE
+COPY LICENSE /usr/share/licenses/xmrig/LICENSE.packaging-MIT
```

and update the two references in `NOTICE`:

```diff
-License; see LICENSE.
+License; see LICENSE.packaging-MIT, alongside this file.
...
-    LICENSE    — upstream XMRig GPL-3.0 licence text
+    LICENSE.xmrig-GPL-3.0     — upstream XMRig GPL-3.0 licence text
+    LICENSE.packaging-MIT     — this repository's MIT licence, for the packaging
     donate.h   — the modified file, as compiled
     NOTICE     — this file
```

## Resolution
Dockerfile ships LICENSE.xmrig-GPL-3.0 and LICENSE.packaging-MIT under /usr/share/licenses/xmrig/; NOTICE's two references updated to the new names. Verified in the rebuilt image: LICENSE.xmrig-GPL-3.0 starts 'GNU GENERAL PUBLIC LICENSE', LICENSE.packaging-MIT starts 'MIT License'.
title: Inside the image, NOTICE's 'see LICENSE' pointer for the MIT terms resolves to the GPL text

body:
## Problem

Every deployment path this repository ships caps memory at 2 GiB:

- `deployment.yaml:49-51` — `limits: memory: "2Gi"` (and `requests: memory: "1Gi"`)
- `docker-compose.yml:20-22` — `limits: memory: 2G`
- `README.md:66-70` — `docker run ... --memory 2g`

RandomX in fast mode — the mode xmrig selects here — allocates a 2080 MiB
dataset plus a 256 MiB cache. That is **2336 MiB**, which is **288 MiB more than
the 2048 MiB the manifests permit**. The miner cannot run inside its own
documented limits.

This is not a tuning preference. It is the image's primary function failing
under the image's own reference configuration.

## Evidence

All measured against the image built from this repository at `Dockerfile` HEAD,
on an 8-thread / 62.6 GiB host, using the shipped `config.json`.

**The allocation is fixed and does not adapt to the limit.** Identical in every
run, at every ceiling:

```
randomx  allocated 2336 MB (2080+256) huge pages 0% 0/1168 +JIT
```

**Kubernetes case — swap is off on kubelet nodes by default, so the cgroup
limit is a hard wall:**

```
$ docker run -d --cpus 1 --memory 2g --memory-swap 2g xmrig:audit \
    /bin/xmrig -c /etc/xmrig/config.json --bench=1M
$ docker inspect bench-noswap --format \
    'OOMKilled={{.State.OOMKilled}} Running={{.State.Running}} ExitCode={{.State.ExitCode}}'
OOMKilled=true Running=false ExitCode=137
```

The last line it logged before the kernel killed it:

```
randomx  init dataset algo rx/0 (8 threads) seed 0000000000000000...
randomx  allocated 2336 MB (2080+256) huge pages 0% 0/1168 +JIT (1 ms)
```

It dies during dataset initialisation, every time, before mining a single hash.

**Docker case — the default `--memory 2g` permits 2× swap, so instead of dying
it thrashes.** Same command at 2 GiB versus 3 GiB:

| | `--memory 2g` | `--memory 3g` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| resident | 1.754 GiB / 2 GiB (87.7%) | 2.304 GiB / 3 GiB (76.8%) |
| CPU utilisation | **2.77%** | **100.65%** |
| dataset init | **95 086 ms** | 32 399 ms |
| hashes in first 60 s | **4** | **17 867** |

A ~4,500× hashrate difference, and the 2 GiB container cannot even consume the
one CPU it was given — it is blocked on page faults, not computing.

The 2 GiB container never reports an error. It logs `dataset ready`, prints
`cpu READY threads 4/4`, serves `/2/summary`, and passes the `HEALTHCHECK`:

```
$ docker inspect --format '{{.State.Health.Status}}' <cid>
healthy
```

**Requests make the Kubernetes case worse.** `deployment.yaml:57` requests only
`1Gi` while limiting to `2Gi`, so the scheduler will place this pod on a node
with 1 GiB free and the pod is OOM-killed even sooner.

## Impact

- **Kubernetes:** CrashLoopBackOff forever. The manifest as shipped cannot start
  the workload.
- **Docker/Compose:** the miner appears healthy and produces effectively nothing,
  which is the worse outcome — the liveness signal, the readiness probe and the
  healthcheck all report success while the hashrate is ~0.07 H/s.
- `README.md:127` currently tells the reader the opposite: "Left as shipped,
  xmrig runs correctly at a lower hashrate rather than failing." At 2 GiB it does
  not run correctly, and on Kubernetes it does fail.

## Fix

**1. Raise the ceiling above the real working set** in all three places. 2336 MiB
allocation + ~50 MiB runtime, rounded to 3 GiB (736 MiB headroom):

`deployment.yaml`:

```yaml
          resources:
            limits:
              # RandomX fast mode allocates 2080 MiB (dataset) + 256 MiB (cache)
              # = 2336 MiB, regardless of this limit — xmrig sizes it from HOST
              # memory, not from the cgroup. Below ~2.4Gi the pod is OOM-killed
              # during dataset init (verified: exit 137). Do not lower this
              # without switching RandomX to light mode as well.
              memory: "3Gi"
              cpu: "1"
              ephemeral-storage: "512Mi"
            requests:
              # Must match the limit: a 1Gi request lets the scheduler place the
              # pod on a node that cannot satisfy the 2336 MiB it will allocate.
              memory: "3Gi"
              cpu: "1"
              ephemeral-storage: "512Mi"
```

`docker-compose.yml`: `memory: 3G`. `README.md`: `--memory 3g`, and correct the
"runs correctly at a lower hashrate" sentence to name the 2336 MiB floor.

**2. Or, if 2 GiB is a hard constraint,** opt into light mode explicitly rather
than letting fast mode be chosen and then starved — `config.json`:

```json
  "randomx": {
    "mode": "light",
```

Light mode uses the 256 MiB cache only and fits comfortably, at roughly a tenth
of fast-mode hashrate. That is a legitimate trade, but it must be a stated
choice; today the config asks for fast mode and the manifests deny it the memory.

**3. Add the floor to the `README.md` Performance tuning table** so the
constraint is documented where the other memory-shaped options already are:

| Option | Requires |
| --- | --- |
| `randomx.mode: auto`/`fast` (default) | **≥ 2336 MiB** of container memory (2080 MiB dataset + 256 MiB cache). Below this the container is OOM-killed on Kubernetes, or swap-thrashes to ~0 H/s under Docker. |

## Resolution
Raised the ceiling to 3Gi/3G/3g in deployment.yaml, docker-compose.yml and the README docker run recipe, and set requests.memory == limits.memory so the scheduler cannot place the pod on a node that cannot satisfy the 2336 MiB it will allocate. Added a memory table to README Performance tuning giving the 2336 MiB floor and the light-mode alternative, and replaced the false 'runs correctly at a lower hashrate' sentence. Verified on the rebuilt image at --memory 3g --memory-swap 3g (the no-swap Kubernetes case that previously gave OOMKilled=true exit 137): OOMKilled=false, still running, 2.292GiB/3GiB (76.4%), CPU 93.86% vs 2.77% before, dataset ready in 21146 ms vs 95086 ms.
title: The 2 GiB memory ceiling in every reference deployment is 288 MiB below what RandomX needs: the pod is OOM-killed on Kubernetes and thrashes at 1/4500 hashrate under Docker

## Problem

`README.md:49-51` documents that the pool `user` (default `${HOSTNAME}`) is sent
to the pool in cleartext, and offers two mitigations: set an explicit value, "or
enable `tls`". The only `tls` key a reader can find is the top-level block in
`config.json:45-47`. That block does not encrypt the pool connection — it
configures TLS for xmrig's own HTTP API server. A user who follows the advice
believes their identifier is now encrypted in transit. It is not.

## Evidence

Top-level `tls` is consumed only by the HTTP server. XMRig v6.22.2,
`src/base/api/Httpd.cpp:73`:

```cpp
tls = m_http->setTls(m_base->config()->tls());
```

Pool TLS is a completely separate, per-pool flag.
`src/base/net/stratum/Pool.h:98`:

```cpp
inline bool isTLS() const  { return m_flags.test(FLAG_TLS) || m_url.isTLS(); }
```

set from the `"tls"` key *inside* a pool object (`Pool.h:72 static const char
*kTls;`) or from a `stratum+ssl://` URL scheme.

The repository's `config.json` has no per-pool `tls` key — only the top-level
block, which is the one the README's wording sends the reader to.

## Impact

Silent failure of a security control the documentation promises. Setting
`"tls": {"enabled": true}` at the top level leaves the pool login (containing
the worker identifier, and for a normal Monero deployment the payout address)
travelling in cleartext exactly as before, while additionally putting the HTTP
API into a TLS mode with no certificate configured.

## Fix

In `README.md`, name the per-pool key explicitly and disambiguate the top-level
block:

```markdown
  - user: your-miner-identifier. Defaults to `${HOSTNAME}`, which xmrig expands
    to the container hostname and sends to the pool **in cleartext** — set an
    explicit value if you do not want that, or set `"tls": true` *inside the
    pool object* (not the top-level `tls` block, which configures the HTTP
    API's own TLS) if your pool offers a TLS port.
```

Add a matching comment next to the top-level block's entry in the README so the
two `tls` keys are never confused again.

## Resolution
README now says to set "tls": true INSIDE the pool object and explicitly states that the top-level tls block configures xmrig's own HTTP API and does nothing for the pool connection. Confirmed against xmrig v6.22.2: Httpd.cpp:73 consumes config()->tls(), Pool.h:98 isTLS() reads the per-pool flag.
title: README tells users to "enable tls" to protect the pool user, but the tls block it points at is the HTTP API server, not the pool

## Problem

`verify` is described at `.github/workflows/build.yaml:35-40` as the job that
gates publication because it "actually runs the binary". It runs the binary with
the image's `CMD` **overridden**:

```yaml
out="$(docker run --rm xmrig:ci /bin/xmrig --version)"
```

`--version` prints a string and exits. It never reads `/etc/xmrig/config.json`,
never starts the HTTP API, and never exercises the `HEALTHCHECK`. Three
load-bearing parts of the image contract have no coverage at all.

## Evidence

The untested surface, all of which the image ships and the manifests depend on:

- `Dockerfile:78` — `CMD ["/bin/xmrig", "-c", "/etc/xmrig/config.json"]`. A
  `config.json` that xmrig rejects (bad JSON, an unknown key in a strict block,
  a malformed pool entry) produces an image that exits immediately on every
  start. CI is green.
- `Dockerfile:75-76` — the `HEALTHCHECK` wget against `:8080`. It depends on
  `config.json`'s `http.enabled`, `http.host: 0.0.0.0` and `http.port: 8080`
  (`config.json:22-28`) all staying as they are, and on xmrig being built with
  `WITH_HTTP`. Flip any one and every container reports unhealthy forever —
  CI still passes.
- `deployment.yaml:65-76` — liveness and readiness probes hit the same `:8080`
  `/2/summary` path. Same exposure: a config change that closes the API turns
  every pod into a CrashLoopBackOff, and nothing upstream of the cluster catches
  it.

That the whole path does work today is exactly what makes the gap invisible;
verified by hand against the built image:

```
$ docker run -d --cpus 1 --memory 2g xmrig:audit      # default CMD, no override
$ docker exec <cid> sh -c 'wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:8080/2/summary >/dev/null'; echo $?
0
$ docker inspect --format '{{.State.Health.Status}}' <cid>
healthy
```

Nothing in CI performs those three commands.

## Impact

The job the workflow calls the publication gate validates one string. Any
regression in the config, the API wiring, the healthcheck, or the `WITH_HTTP`
build option ships to `:latest` with a green pipeline.

## Fix

Extend the existing `Smoke test` step in `.github/workflows/build.yaml` to run
the image as shipped, after the `--version` assertion:

```yaml
      - name: Smoke test the image as shipped
        run: |
          cid="$(docker run -d xmrig:ci)"          # default CMD, default config
          trap 'docker rm -f "$cid" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true' EXIT
          for _ in $(seq 30); do
            docker exec "$cid" sh -c 'wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:8080/2/summary' \
              >/tmp/summary.json 2>/dev/null && break
            sleep 1
          done
          test -s /tmp/summary.json || {
            echo "::error::image did not serve /2/summary within 30s"
            docker logs "$cid"; exit 1
          }
          # the config was parsed and the API is wired as the probes expect
          grep -q '"restricted":true' /tmp/summary.json || {
            echo "::error::HTTP API is not in restricted mode"; exit 1; }
          # the container's own HEALTHCHECK agrees
          docker exec "$cid" sh -c \
            'wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:8080/2/summary >/dev/null 2>&1' || {
            echo "::error::HEALTHCHECK command failed inside the image"; exit 1; }
```

This runs on both matrix platforms and costs a few seconds. It would have caught
every failure mode listed above.

## Resolution
Added a 'Smoke test the image as shipped' step to verify: starts the container with its own CMD and default config, polls /2/summary for 30s, asserts restricted mode, then runs the HEALTHCHECK command verbatim. Runs on both matrix platforms. Verified locally against the rebuilt image: 3/3 PASS. The first draft asserted '"restricted":true' and failed - xmrig pretty-prints its JSON - so the committed version matches whitespace-tolerantly with grep -qE. That bug was only visible by running the step, which is the point of the finding.
title: The gating CI job never runs the image as shipped: the default CMD, config.json and HEALTHCHECK are all untested

body:
## Problem

`Dockerfile:5-8` pins Alpine by digest and states why:

```
# Digest-pinned: `alpine:3.24` alone is a floating tag, republished on every
# 3.24.x patch, so the same commit would otherwise build different images.
```

The same reasoning applies with more force to the thing this image exists to
ship, and is not applied there. `Dockerfile:20-21`:

```dockerfile
RUN test -n "${XMRIG_VERSION}" && \
  git clone --depth 1 --branch "${XMRIG_VERSION}" https://github.com/xmrig/xmrig.git /xmrig
```

`--branch v6.22.2` resolves a Git **tag**, which is a mutable pointer. Anyone
with push access to `xmrig/xmrig` — or anyone who compromises it — can move
`v6.22.2` to a different commit, and every subsequent build of this unchanged
Dockerfile compiles and publishes different source under the same version label.
Nothing in the repository or the pipeline would notice.

## Evidence

Tag mutability is directly observable: `git ls-remote --tags` returns whatever
object the tag currently points at, and GitHub permits `git push --force
--tags`. The build has no commit pin and no signature check.

The verification that does exist does not cover this. `.github/workflows/build.yaml:65-74`
asserts only the version *string* the binary prints:

```bash
out="$(docker run --rm xmrig:ci /bin/xmrig --version)"
echo "$out" | grep -q "$expected"
```

A moved tag keeps `APP_VERSION` at `6.22.2`, so that assertion still passes. The
`donate.h` grep guards at `Dockerfile:25-28` likewise check only the two donate
constants.

This is a cryptocurrency miner: the published artifact holds a pool address and
runs unattended on other people's machines. It is a high-value target for
exactly this substitution.

## Impact

The repository's stated reproducibility guarantee ("the same commit would
otherwise build different images") does not hold for 99% of the image's content
by value. A silent upstream tag move changes the shipped miner binary with a
green pipeline and an unchanged repository.

## Fix

Pin the commit alongside the tag and fail the build if they disagree. In
`Dockerfile`, next to the existing renovate annotation:

```dockerfile
# renovate: datasource=github-tags depName=xmrig/xmrig
ARG XMRIG_VERSION="v6.22.2"
# The commit v6.22.2 pointed at when it was pinned. A tag is a mutable pointer;
# this is not. Update both together.
ARG XMRIG_COMMIT="<full 40-char sha of refs/tags/v6.22.2^{commit}>"
```

and in the builder stage, replace the bare clone with a verified one:

```dockerfile
ARG XMRIG_VERSION
ARG XMRIG_COMMIT
RUN test -n "${XMRIG_VERSION}" && test -n "${XMRIG_COMMIT}" && \
  git clone --depth 1 --branch "${XMRIG_VERSION}" https://github.com/xmrig/xmrig.git /xmrig && \
  actual="$(git -C /xmrig rev-parse HEAD)" && \
  { [ "${actual}" = "${XMRIG_COMMIT}" ] || \
    { echo "tag ${XMRIG_VERSION} moved: expected ${XMRIG_COMMIT}, got ${actual}"; exit 1; }; }
```

Obtain the SHA with:

```bash
git ls-remote https://github.com/xmrig/xmrig.git 'refs/tags/v6.22.2^{}'
```

Renovate bumps `XMRIG_VERSION`; the `XMRIG_COMMIT` line then fails the build
until it is updated in the same commit, which is the intended forcing function.

## Resolution
Added ARG XMRIG_COMMIT=f9e990d0f0167c92d09334213ac6950033bbbba1 (resolved via git ls-remote, cross-checked against a real clone's HEAD) and a git rev-parse HEAD comparison after the clone that fails the build on a mismatch. Negative test performed: docker build --build-arg XMRIG_COMMIT=0000... exits 1 with 'upstream tag v6.22.2 moved: expected 0000..., got f9e990d0...'. Renovate still bumps XMRIG_VERSION; the guard then forces XMRIG_COMMIT to be updated in the same commit.
title: XMRig is fetched by mutable git tag while the base image is digest-pinned, contradicting the reproducibility rationale the Dockerfile states for Alpine

## Problem

`README.md:62-70`, `docker-compose.yml:18-22` and `deployment.yaml:48-59` all
cap the miner with `--cpus`/`limits.cpu` and `--memory`/`limits.memory`. Both
are CFS quota and cgroup memory limits. XMRig reads neither. It sizes its
thread count from the host's hwloc topology and picks its RandomX mode from the
host's *total* RAM, then runs that plan inside a far smaller box.

## Evidence

Built from this repository at `Dockerfile` HEAD and run with the README's exact
recipe on an 8-thread / 62.6 GiB host:

```
$ docker run -d --cpus 1 --memory 2g xmrig:audit
$ docker exec <cid> wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:8080/2/summary
```

The miner's own view of its machine:

```json
"cpu":       {"brand":"Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-7700 CPU @ 3.60GHz",
              "cores":4,"threads":8,"packages":1,"nodes":1,"l3":8388608},
"resources": {"memory":{"free":50933317632,"total":67233918976}}
```

`total` is 62.6 GiB — the host's — inside a container limited to 2 GiB. The
startup banner agrees:

```
 * CPU     Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-7700 CPU @ 3.60GHz (1) 64-bit AES
              L2:1.0 MB L3:8.0 MB 4C/8T NUMA:1
 * MEMORY  15.3/62.6 GB (24%)
```

Neither the 1-CPU quota nor the 2 GiB limit appears anywhere in what xmrig
believes about its environment.

## Impact

Two compounding failures on any host bigger than the limit:

1. **Threads.** xmrig plans one mining thread per eligible host core (4 here,
   but 64 on a 64-core node) and schedules them all into a single CPU of quota.
   The threads spend their lives being throttled and context-switched; the
   effective hashrate is far below what one dedicated core would deliver.
2. **Memory.** The RandomX mode decision is made against 62.6 GiB of "available"
   memory, so xmrig selects fast mode and its 2080 MiB dataset — see the
   companion finding on the 2 GiB ceiling.

`--cpus`/`limits.cpu` therefore do not do what `README.md:62` claims they do
("Set a limit. Without one xmrig takes every core on the host"). They bound the
*CPU time consumed*, but not the *number of threads created*, which is the
thing that actually has to be sized.

## Fix

Use a CPU **set**, not a quota — hwloc honours the process affinity mask, so
xmrig sees exactly the CPUs it is given:

`README.md`:

```bash
docker run -dit --rm \
    --cpuset-cpus 0 --memory 3g \
    --volume "$(pwd)"/config.json:/etc/xmrig/config.json:ro \
    --name xmrig ivuorinen/docker-xmrig:latest
```

`docker-compose.yml`:

```yaml
    cpuset: "0"
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          memory: 3G
```

Kubernetes has no cpuset field on a container; document the two options that do
work there and pick one in the manifest:

- give the pod Guaranteed QoS **and** run the kubelet with
  `--cpu-manager-policy=static` so integer CPU limits become exclusive cores; or
- leave the quota and pin the thread count in `config.json` instead, e.g.
  `"cpu": { "max-threads-hint": 100, "rx": [0] }`, so the miner's plan matches
  the quota regardless of host size.

Whichever is chosen, `README.md`'s "Set a limit" section must say that a CPU
quota alone does not reduce xmrig's thread count.

## Resolution
docker-compose.yml now uses cpuset: "0" instead of a cpus quota, and the README docker run recipe uses --cpuset-cpus 0, both with a comment explaining that hwloc honours the affinity mask but cannot see a CFS quota. deployment.yaml carries a comment on requests.cpu stating that Kubernetes has no cpuset field and naming the two things that do work (static CPU manager policy, or pinning threads in config.json). Verified: with --cpuset-cpus 0 the rebuilt image reports '1C/1T' and 'use profile rx (1 thread)', where it previously reported 4C/8T and started 4 threads.
title: CPU and memory limits in every reference deployment are cgroup quotas xmrig cannot see; it sizes itself from host topology and host RAM

## Problem

`deployment.yaml:103-114` ships a deny-all-ingress NetworkPolicy, and
`README.md:33-35` presents it as the answer to the tokenless HTTP API:

> Do not route it off the node. `deployment.yaml` ships a `NetworkPolicy` that
> denies pod ingress

NetworkPolicy is enforced by the CNI plugin, not by Kubernetes. On a cluster
whose CNI has no policy engine — plain Flannel, kindnet, several managed
defaults — the API server accepts the object, `kubectl get networkpolicy` shows
it, and nothing anywhere enforces it. There is no error, no event, no warning.

## Evidence

`deployment.yaml:108-114`:

```yaml
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: xmrig
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
  ingress: []
```

Kubernetes accepts and stores this object unconditionally; enforcement is
delegated to the network plugin. Nothing in the repository states the
prerequisite, and the README's wording ("ships a NetworkPolicy that denies pod
ingress") reads as a guarantee.

What is behind it, confirmed against the built image, is a genuinely
unauthenticated endpoint. From the running container:

```json
{"restricted": true,
 "worker_id": "1f2ca66df1cb",
 "cpu": {"brand":"Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-7700 CPU @ 3.60GHz","cores":4,"threads":8},
 "resources": {"memory":{"free":50933317632,"total":67233918976}}}
```

no token required — host CPU model, host free/total memory, and the pod
hostname, plus the pool `user` once connected.

## Impact

On a non-enforcing CNI the only control standing between every pod in the
cluster and that endpoint does nothing, and the documentation actively tells the
operator it is covered. This is worse than shipping no policy at all, because it
converts a known risk into an assumed-handled one.

## Fix

State the prerequisite where the control is claimed. In `deployment.yaml`,
extend the existing comment above the NetworkPolicy:

```yaml
# REQUIRES a CNI that enforces NetworkPolicy (Calico, Cilium, Antrea, Weave,
# or a managed equivalent). Plain Flannel and kindnet accept this object and
# silently ignore it — verify with a connectivity test, not with `kubectl get
# networkpolicy`.
```

In `README.md`, change "ships a `NetworkPolicy` that denies pod ingress" to say
the policy only takes effect on a policy-enforcing CNI, and give the one-line
check:

```bash
kubectl run np-probe --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox -n xmrig -- \
  wget -qO- --timeout=5 http://<pod-ip>:8080/2/summary && echo "POLICY NOT ENFORCED"
```

## Resolution
Documented the CNI prerequisite in both places the control is claimed: deployment.yaml's NetworkPolicy comment now states that enforcement is the network plugin's job, that plain Flannel and kindnet accept and silently ignore the object, and that 'kubectl get networkpolicy' is not evidence; the README repeats it and both give the same busybox connectivity probe to verify enforcement for real.
title: The NetworkPolicy that is documented as the control protecting the tokenless API is a silent no-op on clusters whose CNI does not enforce NetworkPolicy

body:
## Problem

`deployment.yaml:43-47` hardens the container properly:

```yaml
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            capabilities:
              drop: ["ALL"]
```

`docker-compose.yml` applies none of it, and neither does the `docker run`
recipe at `README.md:66-70`. The README presents the three as interchangeable
deployment paths ("Deploy the image as a standalone Docker container or to a
Kubernetes cluster", `README.md:57`), so a reader has no way to tell that two of
them drop every one of those controls.

## Evidence

`docker-compose.yml` in full contains `image`, `volumes`, `restart`, `deploy`
and `logging` — no `cap_drop`, no `read_only`, no `security_opt`. Confirmed
against the built image: the Compose-equivalent container keeps the full default
capability set and a writable root filesystem, while the Kubernetes pod for the
same image has neither.

The drift is not theoretical for this image specifically: it runs an
internet-facing process that maintains a long-lived outbound connection to a
third-party pool and parses attacker-influenced JSON from it. That is precisely
the workload where `no-new-privileges` and a read-only root filesystem earn
their keep.

## Impact

Anyone deploying via Compose or the documented `docker run` — the two paths the
README puts first — silently gets a materially weaker container than the
Kubernetes path, with nothing in the docs flagging the difference.

## Fix

`docker-compose.yml`:

```yaml
services:
  xmrig:
    image: ivuorinen/docker-xmrig:latest
    read_only: true
    cap_drop: ["ALL"]
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
```

`README.md` `docker run` example:

```bash
docker run -dit --rm \
    --cpuset-cpus 0 --memory 3g \
    --read-only --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges \
    --volume "$(pwd)"/config.json:/etc/xmrig/config.json:ro \
    --name xmrig ivuorinen/docker-xmrig:latest
```

`read_only: true` is safe here: `config.json` is already mounted `:ro`,
`autosave` is `false` (`config.json:2`), and `/log` is a separate writable bind
mount.

## Resolution
docker-compose.yml now sets read_only: true, cap_drop: [ALL] and security_opt: [no-new-privileges:true]; the README docker run recipe gained --read-only --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges with a note on why each is safe here. Verified twice: 'docker compose config' reports all three applied, and a live container run with the same flags starts cleanly, serves /2/summary and exits 0 - so the hardening costs nothing at runtime.
title: Compose and docker run references ship none of the container hardening deployment.yaml applies

## Problem

`.dockerignore:1-3` opens with a statement of what the build context is for:

```
# Only config.json and NOTICE are COPYed into the image; everything else here is
# build-context weight (.git is 55 commits of history, uploaded on every build,
# for both matrix platforms).
```

Three files are copied from the context, not two. `Dockerfile:56`, `:65`, `:66`:

```dockerfile
COPY config.json /etc/xmrig/config.json
COPY NOTICE /usr/share/licenses/xmrig/NOTICE
COPY LICENSE /usr/share/licenses/xmrig/LICENSE.packaging-MIT
```

## Evidence

All three are present in the built image:

```
$ docker run --rm --entrypoint /bin/busybox xmrig:audit ls -l /usr/share/licenses/xmrig/
-rw-rw-r--    1 root     root          1070 LICENSE.packaging-MIT
-rw-r--r--    1 root     root         35141 LICENSE.xmrig-GPL-3.0
-rw-rw-r--    1 root     root          1903 NOTICE
-rw-r--r--    1 root     root          1906 donate.h
```

`LICENSE.packaging-MIT` is the repository's `LICENSE`, copied from the build
context. (`LICENSE.xmrig-GPL-3.0` and `donate.h` come `--from=builder`, so they
are correctly outside this comment's scope.)

`LICENSE` survives today only because it has no extension and so is not caught
by the `*.md` pattern — by luck, not by intent.

## Impact

The comment is the file's own specification of what must not be excluded, and it
is wrong. Someone tidying the context on the strength of it — adding `LICENSE`,
or broadening `*.md` to a catch-all for non-source files — breaks
`Dockerfile:66` with a `COPY failed` at build time. Worse, if the same tidy-up
also touched `NOTICE`, the image would silently stop conveying the GPL-3.0
attribution that `NOTICE` and `README.md:188-194` commit to shipping.

## Fix

`.dockerignore`:

```
# config.json, NOTICE and LICENSE are COPYed into the image (Dockerfile:56,65,66)
# — do not exclude them. Everything below is build-context weight (.git is 55
# commits of history, uploaded on every build, for both matrix platforms).
```

## Resolution
The .dockerignore header now names all three COPYed files (config.json, NOTICE, LICENSE with their Dockerfile line numbers) and warns that LICENSE escapes the *.md rule only because it has no extension.
title: The .dockerignore header lists the files copied into the image and omits LICENSE, which the Dockerfile does copy

## Problem

Three keys in `config.json` describe behaviour that is unreachable in this
image. A previous audit already removed the `opencl`/`cuda` blocks for exactly
this reason (`audit-41502170`, resolved); these were left.

```json
  "dmi": true,               // config.json:41
  "pause-on-battery": false, // config.json:51
  "pause-on-active": false,  // config.json:52
```

## Evidence

**`dmi`** — xmrig's Unix DMI reader reads two sysfs paths
(`src/hw/dmi/DmiReader_unix.cpp:46-47`):

```cpp
static const char *kSysEntryFile = "/sys/firmware/dmi/tables/smbios_entry_point";
static const char *kSysTableFile = "/sys/firmware/dmi/tables/DMI";
```

Neither is present in the container, and the process is uid 10001 regardless:

```
$ docker run --rm --entrypoint /bin/busybox xmrig:audit sh -c \
    'ls -l /sys/firmware/dmi/tables/; head -c 16 /sys/firmware/dmi/tables/DMI'
ls: /sys/firmware/dmi/tables/: No such file or directory
UNREADABLE
```

Confirmed absent from the API output too — the running container's
`/2/summary` has no `dmi` member at all.

**`pause-on-battery`** requires a battery/AC power source to detect;
**`pause-on-active`** requires an input-idle signal from a desktop session.
Neither exists in a headless container, and both are already at their upstream
defaults, so they change nothing even where they could apply.

## Impact

No runtime effect — this is a clarity defect. Three keys imply the image
supports behaviour it cannot, which is what makes the *other* keys in the file
hard to trust: a reader cannot tell which entries are load-bearing (`autosave`,
`randomx.rdmsr`, `randomx.wrmsr`, `http.*`) and which are decoration. The
`README.md:119-126` tuning table sets the precedent by documenting exactly what
each privileged option needs; these three are not in it.

## Fix

Delete the three keys from `config.json`. They are upstream defaults, so
removing them changes no behaviour:

```diff
   "print-time": 60,
   "health-print-time": 60,
-  "dmi": true,
   "retries": 5,
   "retry-pause": 5,
@@
   "watch": true,
-  "pause-on-battery": false,
-  "pause-on-active": false
 }
```

Keep the remaining defaults that the `README.md` tuning table references
(`randomx.1gb-pages`, `randomx.cache_qos`, `cpu.huge-pages`) — those are
documented knobs, not decoration.

## Resolution
Removed dmi, pause-on-battery and pause-on-active from config.json (43 keys -> 19 top-level; all were upstream defaults, so no behaviour change). dmi was confirmed unreachable: /sys/firmware/dmi/tables does not exist in the container and the API emits no dmi member.
title: config.json enables dmi and ships two desktop-only pause keys that cannot do anything in this container

body:
## Problem

The same pin appears twice, independently editable. `Dockerfile:8`:

```dockerfile
FROM alpine:3.24@sha256:28bd5fe8b56d1bd048e5babf5b10710ebe0bae67db86916198a6eec434943f8b AS builder
```

`Dockerfile:35`:

```dockerfile
FROM alpine:3.24@sha256:28bd5fe8b56d1bd048e5babf5b10710ebe0bae67db86916198a6eec434943f8b
```

Nothing enforces that they match. The Dockerfile itself flags this exact hazard
two lines above the first one (`Dockerfile:14-16`):

> do not add the edge repository, it makes builds unpinned and **splits the ABI
> between this stage and the runtime stage**

That is the failure mode a divergent digest produces, by a different route.

## Evidence

`xmrig` is compiled in the builder stage against musl, libuv, hwloc and OpenSSL,
then the bare binary is copied into a separately-resolved runtime stage
(`Dockerfile:55`):

```dockerfile
COPY --from=builder /xmrig/build/xmrig /bin/xmrig
```

It is dynamically linked against all of them:

```
$ docker run --rm --entrypoint /lib/ld-musl-x86_64.so.1 xmrig:audit --list /bin/xmrig
	libssl.so.3 => /usr/lib/libssl.so.3
	libcrypto.so.3 => /usr/lib/libcrypto.so.3
	libuv.so.1 => /usr/lib/libuv.so.1
	libhwloc.so.15 => /usr/lib/libhwloc.so.15
	libc.musl-x86_64.so.1 => /lib/ld-musl-x86_64.so.1
```

If the two digests ever differ across a musl or soname bump, the binary compiles
cleanly in one stage and fails to resolve symbols in the other — at container
start, not at build time, and therefore after publication.

## Impact

A hand-edit to one `FROM` and not the other, or a partially-applied Renovate
patch, produces a mismatch that no build-time check catches. The repository has
already invested in digest pinning specifically to make builds deterministic;
duplicating the pin reintroduces a way for the two halves to drift apart.

## Fix

Resolve the base once and derive both stages from it, so the digest is
single-sourced and the two stages are the same image by construction:

```dockerfile
# Digest-pinned: `alpine:3.24` alone is a floating tag, republished on every
# 3.24.x patch, so the same commit would otherwise build different images.
# Renovate bumps the digest. Declared once — the builder and the runtime stage
# MUST be the same base, or the binary compiled in one links against a
# different musl/libuv/hwloc/OpenSSL than the one that runs it.
FROM alpine:3.24@sha256:28bd5fe8b56d1bd048e5babf5b10710ebe0bae67db86916198a6eec434943f8b AS base

FROM base AS builder
...

FROM base
```

Renovate's `dockerfile` manager updates the single remaining `FROM` line exactly
as it does today.

## Resolution
The Alpine digest is now declared once as 'FROM alpine:3.24@sha256:... AS base'; the builder stage is 'FROM base AS builder' and the runtime stage is 'FROM base', so the two cannot diverge. The comment explains that the binary is compiled in one stage and copied into the other, which is why they must be the same image. Renovate still sees exactly one FROM line to bump.
title: The Alpine digest is written out twice and the two copies must stay byte-identical or the build and runtime stages split their ABI

body:
## Problem

A tagged release runs the xmrig compile four separate times, with nothing shared
between them:

| Job | Platform | Compile |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `verify` (`build.yaml:58-64`) | linux/amd64 | full |
| `verify` (`build.yaml:58-64`) | linux/arm64 | full |
| `build` (`build.yaml:132-139`) | linux/amd64 | full, identical to verify's |
| `build` (`build.yaml:132-139`) | linux/arm64 | full, identical to verify's |

Neither `docker/build-push-action` step sets `cache-from` or `cache-to`, so the
`build` job rebuilds byte-for-byte what `verify` compiled minutes earlier in the
same workflow run, on the same platform, from the same context.

## Evidence

The compile is the entire cost of this image. From a local build of this
Dockerfile:

```
#11 [builder 5/5] RUN cmake .. -DWITH_OPENCL=OFF -DWITH_CUDA=OFF && make -j"$(nproc)"
#11 104.3 [100%] Built target xmrig
#11 DONE 106.2s
```

106 seconds with `-j8`. Every other step in the build is trivial by comparison:

```
#10 DONE 1.5s   #12 DONE 1.9s   #13 DONE 1.7s   #14 DONE 1.6s
#15 DONE 2.3s   #16 DONE 1.3s   #17 DONE 1.3s   #18 DONE 2.7s
```

GitHub-hosted runners have far fewer cores than the 8 used above, so each of the
four compiles costs several minutes of wall clock, and `build` cannot start
until `verify` finishes (`build.yaml:85-86`, `needs: verify`) — the two halves
are serial, not parallel.

## Impact

Release wall-clock and CI minutes are roughly double what they need to be. The
cost is paid on every tag, and it is pure duplication: the `build` job's compile
has no input that `verify`'s did not already have.

## Fix

Add a GitHub Actions cache to both steps. Cache scope is per workflow run, so
`build` picks up exactly what `verify` produced:

`verify` → `Build for test`:

```yaml
        with:
          context: .
          platforms: ${{ matrix.platform }}
          load: true
          tags: xmrig:ci
          cache-from: type=gha,scope=${{ matrix.platform }}
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max,scope=${{ matrix.platform }}
```

`build` → `Build and push by digest`:

```yaml
        with:
          context: .
          platforms: ${{ matrix.platform }}
          labels: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.labels }}
          cache-from: type=gha,scope=${{ matrix.platform }}
          outputs: type=image,...
```

The per-platform `scope` matters: without it the amd64 and arm64 matrix legs
share one cache key and evict each other on every run.

**Order this after the mutable-tag finding on `Dockerfile`.** A layer cache keys
on the `RUN git clone --branch "${XMRIG_VERSION}" ...` command string, which does
not change when an upstream tag is moved — so caching would make a moved tag
*stickier*, not just faster. Pin `XMRIG_COMMIT` first; then the verification line
is part of the cache key and a moved tag correctly busts it.

## Resolution
Added cache-from/cache-to type=gha with a per-platform scope to the verify job's build, and cache-from with the same scope to the build job's, so a tagged release compiles twice instead of four times. Per-platform scope prevents the amd64 and arm64 legs evicting each other. Ordered after the XMRIG_COMMIT pin as the finding required: the clone RUN string now contains the commit check, so a moved upstream tag busts the cache rather than being served from it.
title: Every release compiles xmrig four times from scratch because no buildx layer cache is configured

body:
## Problem

`config.json:4-5` keeps xmrig's two terminal-oriented defaults on in an image
whose documented log path is a non-TTY pipe:

```json
  "colors": true,
  "title": true,
```

`README.md:131` states the contract: "This Docker image sends the container logs
to the `stdout`." Those logs are consumed by `docker logs`, `kubectl logs`, and
whatever aggregator sits behind them — none of which is a terminal.

## Evidence

Captured from the image built from this repository, piped through `cat -v` to
make the escapes visible:

```
$ docker run -d --cpus 1 --memory 2g --name xmrig-audit1 xmrig:audit
$ docker logs xmrig-audit1 2>&1 | cat -v | head -3
^[[1;32m * ^[[0m^[[1;37mABOUT        ^[[0m^[[1;36mXMRig/6.22.2^[[0m^[[1;37m gcc/15.2.0^[[0m...
^[[1;32m * ^[[0m^[[1;37mLIBS         libuv/1.52.1 OpenSSL/3.5.7 hwloc/2.12.2^[[0m^[[0m
^[[1;32m * ^[[0m^[[1;37mHUGE PAGES   ^[[0m^[[1;32msupported^[[0m^[[0m
```

Every operational line carries them, including the ones an operator greps for:

```
[2026-08-02 19:58:01^[[1;30m.176^[[0m] ^[[0;31m^[[44;1m^[[1;37m net     ^[[0m
^[[1;36mCHANGE-ME.example:3333^[[0m ^[[0;31mDNS error: ^[[0m^[[1;31m"unknown node or service"^[[0m
```

xmrig emits them unconditionally when `colors` is set; it does not test whether
stdout is a TTY.

## Impact

- `grep 'DNS error'` works, but `grep '^\[2026'` and any anchored or
  field-position pattern does not, because escapes sit between the timestamp and
  its milliseconds.
- Log aggregators (Loki, CloudWatch, Elasticsearch) store and index the escape
  bytes; JSON log shippers escape them again into `[1;32m`, roughly
  doubling the size of every line.
- The `title` escape is an OSC sequence written to a stream nothing will
  interpret.

## Fix

`config.json`:

```json
  "autosave": false,
  "background": false,
  "colors": false,
  "title": false,
```

Note the surrounding keys stay: `autosave: false` is load-bearing for the
read-only config mount, and `background: false` keeps xmrig as PID 1 rather than
daemonising. Add a short comment in `README.md`'s Logging section noting that
colours are off deliberately for aggregation, so a future edit does not
"restore" them.

## Resolution
Set "colors": false and "title": false in config.json and documented in the README Logging section why they are off. Verified on the rebuilt image: 'docker logs | grep -c $'\033'' returns 0, where the previous image emitted escapes on every line including between the timestamp and its milliseconds.
title: colors and title are enabled, so every log line reaches docker logs and kubectl logs full of ANSI escape sequences

body:
## Problem

Two separate defects in the same file.

**1. Prose errors** — `README.md:179` and `README.md:198`:

```
Use at your own disgression. This repository is by no means financial advise to mine
```

`disgression` is not a word (intended: *discretion*), and *advise* is the verb
where the noun *advice* is meant. Both sit in the Disclaimer, which is the one
paragraph in the file whose job is to be read as a careful legal statement.

```
This repo is a based on works of:
```

`is a based on` — stray article.

**2. Declared line-length convention violated.** `.editorconfig:11` sets the
repository-wide rule:

```ini
[*]
max_line_length = 120
```

Seven lines in `README.md` exceed it:

```
$ awk 'length>120 {printf "%s:%d  %d chars\n", FILENAME, NR, length}' README.md
README.md:102  154 chars
README.md:104  160 chars
README.md:105  137 chars
README.md:107  128 chars
README.md:122  148 chars
README.md:124  131 chars
README.md:125  201 chars
```

## Evidence

`README.md` is not a private file. `.github/workflows/build.yaml:186-198`
publishes it as the Docker Hub repository description on every tag:

```yaml
  update_description:
    ...
      - name: Update DockerHub repo description
        uses: peter-evans/dockerhub-description@1b9a80c...
```

So both defects are shipped to the image's public landing page.

The line-length rule is genuinely the repository's own: every other file honours
it. `deployment.yaml`'s longest line is 85 characters, `Dockerfile`'s is 88 —
both well inside 120. `README.md` is the sole file that ignores the setting, and
nothing enforces it (no markdownlint, no editorconfig-checker in CI).

## Impact

Cosmetic, but on the project's public face, and the `.editorconfig` violation
makes a declared repository convention advisory-only in practice.

## Fix

`README.md:179-180`:

```markdown
Use at your own discretion. This repository is by no means financial advice to mine
cryptocurrency. This is a project to learn how to build containerised applications.
```

`README.md:198`:

```markdown
This repo is based on the work of:
```

Reflow lines 102, 104, 105, 107, 122, 124 and 125 to 120 columns. Lines 122-125
are the Performance tuning table — Markdown tables reflow badly, so either move
the long `Requires` cells to footnotes beneath the table, or add a scoped
exemption so the declared rule stays true everywhere else:

```ini
# Markdown tables do not reflow; the tuning table in README.md needs the width.
[*.md]
max_line_length = off
```

Pick one — the current state, where the rule is declared globally and silently
broken in one file, is the option that should not stand.

## Resolution
Fixed 'disgression' -> 'discretion', 'financial advise' -> 'financial advice' and 'is a based on works of' -> 'is based on the work of'. Reflowed the Kubernetes step-3 list using new [deployment.yaml] and [tags] link references, and restructured the Performance tuning table into short cells plus numbered notes. README is now entirely within .editorconfig's 120 columns. Residual, disclosed rather than hidden: .github/workflows/build.yaml:40 is 121 characters - a docker:// action reference pinned by sha256 plus the trailing '# v1.7.12' comment Renovate needs. Neither part can be shortened without weakening the digest pinning convention, so it stands.
title: README has three prose errors and seven lines over the max_line_length the repository declares in .editorconfig

body:
## Problem

`Dockerfile:32` pins exactly the two options that do not matter to this image's
contract, and none of the three that do:

```dockerfile
RUN cmake .. -DWITH_OPENCL=OFF -DWITH_CUDA=OFF && make -j"$(nproc)"
```

Three upstream defaults are load-bearing here:

- **`WITH_HTTP`** (`CMakeLists.txt:13`, default `ON`) — without it there is no
  HTTP API, so `Dockerfile:75-76`'s `HEALTHCHECK` and `deployment.yaml:65-76`'s
  liveness and readiness probes all fail permanently.
- **`WITH_TLS`** (`CMakeLists.txt:15`, default `ON`) — `Dockerfile:46-49`
  installs `libssl3` and justifies it with "xmrig is built WITH_TLS". That
  sentence asserts an upstream default as though it were a local guarantee.
- **`CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE`** — unset. `cmake/flags.cmake:8-9` is what rescues it:

  ```cmake
  if ("${CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE}" STREQUAL "")
      set(CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Release)
  endif()
  ```

  Without that upstream fallback the miner builds at `-O0` instead of `-Ofast`
  (`cmake/flags.cmake:66-69`).

## Evidence

Verified against the image built from this Dockerfile — all three defaults
currently hold:

```
$ docker run --rm xmrig:audit /bin/xmrig --version
XMRig 6.22.2
 built on Aug  2 2026 with GCC 15.2.0
libuv/1.52.1  OpenSSL/3.5.7  hwloc/2.12.2      # WITH_TLS on
$ docker run --rm --entrypoint /lib/ld-musl-x86_64.so.1 xmrig:audit --list /bin/xmrig
	libssl.so.3 => /usr/lib/libssl.so.3
	libcrypto.so.3 => /usr/lib/libcrypto.so.3
$ docker run --rm --entrypoint /bin/busybox xmrig:audit ls -l /bin/xmrig
-rwxr-xr-x  1 root root 4645208 /bin/xmrig       # stripped: Release's -Ofast -s
```

The exposure is that `XMRIG_VERSION` is bumped automatically by Renovate
(`Dockerfile:2`). An upstream default change arrives in a dependency-bump PR
that no human reads closely, and CI cannot catch any of the three: the smoke
test only runs `--version` with the image's `CMD` overridden, so it never
touches the HTTP API and never measures a hashrate.

## Impact

Three silent regressions are reachable through an automated version bump: dead
healthcheck and probes, an unused `libssl3` with a now-false justification
comment, and a miner running orders of magnitude slower with no error.

## Fix

Say what the image depends on rather than inheriting it:

```dockerfile
# Pin every option this image's contract depends on. WITH_HTTP backs the
# HEALTHCHECK and the Kubernetes probes; WITH_TLS is why libssl3 is installed in
# the runtime stage; Release is what makes it -Ofast rather than -O0. All three
# are upstream defaults today — pinned so an automated XMRIG_VERSION bump cannot
# change them silently.
RUN cmake .. \
      -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
      -DWITH_HTTP=ON \
      -DWITH_TLS=ON \
      -DWITH_OPENCL=OFF \
      -DWITH_CUDA=OFF && \
    make -j"$(nproc)"
```

Adding `-DWITH_HTTP=ON` also turns a future upstream default flip into a CMake
error rather than a silently API-less image.

## Resolution
The cmake invocation now pins -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DWITH_HTTP=ON -DWITH_TLS=ON alongside the existing -DWITH_OPENCL=OFF -DWITH_CUDA=OFF, with a comment naming what each one backs (the HEALTHCHECK and probes, the libssl3 apk line, -Ofast over -O0). All three were upstream defaults; pinning them means an automated XMRIG_VERSION bump cannot flip one silently. Rebuild succeeds with the explicit flags.
title: Load-bearing CMake options (WITH_HTTP, WITH_TLS, CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE) are left to upstream defaults while the two harmless ones are pinned

## Problem

Residual gap left open deliberately after fixing `audit-bdf51ba5`. The liveness and
readiness probes prove the process is responsive, not that it is mining.

## Evidence

Measured against the fixed image. A container whose pool is unreachable:

```
$ docker inspect --format '{{.State.Health.Status}}' k8ssim
healthy
$ docker exec k8ssim wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:8080/2/summary | jq -c '{connected:.connection.uptime, pool:.connection.pool, hashrate:.hashrate.total}'
{"connected":0,"pool":"","hashrate":[0.0,0.0,0.0]}
```

The healthcheck passes and the readiness probe would mark the pod Ready, while
`connection.pool` is empty and hashrate is zero. xmrig logs `DNS error` every five
seconds and never exits.

## Impact

A pod that has lost its pool — bad DNS, pool outage, wrong credentials, a typo in
the configMap — reports healthy indefinitely and produces nothing. Nothing in the
repository surfaces it.

## Fix

Deliberately *not* fixed in the probe: making liveness depend on `connection.pool`
turns a pool-side outage into a restart loop, which is worse than the symptom, and
the connected case could not be verified in this environment.

The correct place is external alerting. Scrape the API and alert on the condition:

```bash
wget -qO- http://<pod>:8080/2/summary \
  | jq -e '.connection.pool != "" and (.hashrate.total[0] // 0) > 0'
```

For Prometheus, xmrig does not export a metrics endpoint; use a small exporter or
a blackbox check over the same JSON. Whoever runs this must opt into a threshold
appropriate to their pool's reliability — which is why it is not hardcoded here.

## Resolution
Added an Alerting section to the README: it states plainly that the probes prove responsiveness rather than mining, explains why wiring pool state into liveness would turn a pool outage into a crashloop, and gives the jq check on .connection.pool and .hashrate.total. The probes are deliberately unchanged - the gap is now surfaced in the repository, which was the finding's stated impact ('Nothing in the repository surfaces it'), and the threshold is left to the operator.
title: No signal distinguishes a mining pod from a pod that is Ready at zero hashrate

## Problem

`config.json:19` enables huge pages by default:

```json
  "cpu": { "enabled": true, "huge-pages": true, "yield": true }
```

`README.md:124` documents what that needs:

| `cpu.huge-pages` (on by default) | host `vm.nr_hugepages`, plus `--cap-add IPC_LOCK`. Falls back with a warning if unavailable. |

Both requirements are stated in Docker terms only. On Kubernetes — for which
this repository ships a complete manifest — neither is expressible that way, and
`deployment.yaml` as shipped satisfies neither:

- `deployment.yaml:46-47` drops every capability, including the `IPC_LOCK` the
  table says is required:

  ```yaml
            capabilities:
              drop: ["ALL"]
  ```

- Huge pages are a distinct schedulable resource in Kubernetes
  (`resources.limits.hugepages-2Mi`). `deployment.yaml:48-59` requests none, so
  the pod has no huge-page allocation available regardless of node
  configuration.

## Evidence

Measured against the built image — the fallback path is what actually runs:

```
randomx  allocated 2336 MB (2080+256) huge pages 0% 0/1168 +JIT
cpu      READY threads 4/4 (4) huge pages 0% 0/4 memory 8192 KB
```

`0/1168` and `0/4`: not one huge page was obtained, in a container with the
*full* default capability set. The Kubernetes pod, with `drop: ["ALL"]`, cannot
do better.

The startup banner is actively misleading here, because it reports the host's
capability rather than the container's allocation:

```
 * HUGE PAGES   supported
```

## Impact

The table reads as a menu of things an operator can enable. For the Kubernetes
path it is not: `cpu.huge-pages` is on by default, cannot work under the shipped
manifest, and the only signal is a `0%` buried in the RandomX init line. RandomX
loses roughly 20–30% of its hashrate without huge pages, so this is a real cost
being paid silently by anyone following the Kubernetes instructions.

## Fix

Extend the `README.md:119-126` table to give the Kubernetes requirement
alongside the Docker one:

| Option | Requires |
| --- | --- |
| `cpu.huge-pages` (on by default) | **Docker:** host `vm.nr_hugepages`, plus `--cap-add IPC_LOCK`. **Kubernetes:** node with pre-allocated huge pages, `resources.limits.hugepages-2Mi: "2336Mi"` on the container, and `IPC_LOCK` added back to the otherwise-dropped capability set. The shipped `deployment.yaml` does none of these, so huge pages are off there — verify with `huge pages 0%` in the `randomx allocated` log line. Falls back with a warning if unavailable. |

and add a pointer in `deployment.yaml` next to the capability drop so the two
files stay honest with each other:

```yaml
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            capabilities:
              # Dropping IPC_LOCK disables config.json's `cpu.huge-pages`
              # (~20-30% of RandomX hashrate). Deliberate: re-adding it, plus a
              # hugepages-2Mi limit and a node with pre-allocated pages, is an
              # opt-in — see the Performance tuning table in README.md.
              drop: ["ALL"]
```

## Resolution
README note 2 under the tuning table now gives the Docker and Kubernetes requirements separately, states that the shipped deployment.yaml satisfies neither (no hugepages-2Mi request, IPC_LOCK dropped), quantifies the cost at 20-30% of RandomX hashrate, and gives 'huge pages 0%' as the way to confirm. deployment.yaml's capabilities block carries a matching comment so the two files stay honest with each other.
title: The Performance tuning table gives host-level requirements for huge pages but omits the Kubernetes ones, and the shipped manifest cannot satisfy them at all

## Problem

`NOTICE:29-38` defines the corresponding source for the GPL-3.0 work the image
conveys:

```
The complete corresponding source is:

  * upstream XMRig at the tag recorded in the image's
    org.opencontainers.image.version label, from
    https://github.com/xmrig/xmrig ; plus
  * the modification above, which is the build recipe in this repository's
    Dockerfile.
```

The first bullet carries a URL. The second says "this repository" and never
names it. `NOTICE` ships *inside the image* (`Dockerfile:65`), where "this
repository" has no referent — the reader has a container filesystem, not a
checkout.

## Evidence

The Dockerfile is not conveyed with the image, and NOTICE is the document that
is meant to point at it:

```
$ docker run --rm --entrypoint /bin/busybox xmrig:audit ls /usr/share/licenses/xmrig/
LICENSE.packaging-MIT
LICENSE.xmrig-GPL-3.0
NOTICE
donate.h
```

Nor do the labels close the gap on a locally built image:

```
$ docker inspect xmrig:audit --format '{{json .Config.Labels}}'
{"org.opencontainers.image.licenses":"GPL-3.0-or-later",
 "org.opencontainers.image.version":"v6.22.2"}
```

Only images published through `.github/workflows/build.yaml:117-124` acquire
`org.opencontainers.image.source` and `.revision`, and then only as a side
effect of `docker/metadata-action`'s defaults — nothing in the repository states
that the GPL pointer depends on them.

## Impact

GPLv3 §6 requires the corresponding source to include "the scripts used to
control compilation and installation", and permits a third-party network
location only when accompanied by "clear directions next to the object code
saying where to find the Corresponding Source". The directions for the upstream
half are clear; for the modified half — this repository's build recipe — they
are a pronoun. A recipient holding only the image cannot follow them.

## Fix

Name the repository in `NOTICE`, in both places a reader could start from:

```
The complete corresponding source is:

  * upstream XMRig at the tag recorded in the image's
    org.opencontainers.image.version label, from
    https://github.com/xmrig/xmrig ; plus
  * the build recipe that applies the modification above, in the Dockerfile at
    https://github.com/ivuorinen/docker-xmrig (the exact revision is recorded in
    the image's org.opencontainers.image.revision label).
```

and add the label unconditionally in `Dockerfile`, so it holds for locally built
images too rather than only for pipeline-published ones:

```dockerfile
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.version="${XMRIG_VERSION}" \
  org.opencontainers.image.licenses="GPL-3.0-or-later" \
  org.opencontainers.image.source="https://github.com/ivuorinen/docker-xmrig"
```

## Resolution
NOTICE now names the repository URL for the build recipe half of the corresponding source and points at the .source and .revision labels. Added org.opencontainers.image.source to the Dockerfile LABEL so a locally built image carries the pointer too, not only pipeline-published ones. Verified on the rebuilt image: all three labels present.
title: NOTICE names this repository Dockerfile as part of the GPL corresponding source but gives no location for it

## Problem

`.github/workflows/build.yaml:179` suppresses a specific shellcheck diagnostic:

```yaml
          # shellcheck disable=SC2046  # word splitting is the point: one -t per tag
```

A `shellcheck disable` directive only means something if shellcheck runs. No job
in this repository runs it, or `actionlint`. The `lint` job
(`.github/workflows/build.yaml:25-33`) covers the Dockerfile only.

## Evidence

The suppression is load-bearing — removing it produces real diagnostics, so the
author was clearly linting locally:

```
$ sed 's|^ *# shellcheck disable=SC2046.*$||' .github/workflows/build.yaml \
  | actionlint -shellcheck "$(command -v shellcheck)" -stdin-filename .github/workflows/build.yaml -
.github/workflows/build.yaml:178:9: shellcheck reported issue in this script: SC2046:warning:2:33: Quote this to prevent word splitting
.github/workflows/build.yaml:178:9: shellcheck reported issue in this script: SC2046:warning:3:3: Quote this to prevent word splitting
exit=1
```

The workflow as committed is currently clean:

```
$ actionlint -shellcheck "$(command -v shellcheck)" .github/workflows/build.yaml
$ echo $?
0
```

So the gap is not that the file is broken — it is that nothing keeps it that
way. The workflow contains non-trivial shell that no gate protects: two `sed`
version parsers (`:67`, `:109`), a `jq`-driven `imagetools create` with
deliberate word splitting (`:180-181`), and a glob expansion whose failure mode
is a literal `*` in an image reference (`:181`).

## Impact

The Dockerfile — 78 lines, no logic — is gated. The release pipeline's shell,
where a quoting mistake silently mis-tags or mis-pushes a published image, is
not. A future edit that reintroduces SC2046 elsewhere, or breaks a `sed`
pattern, reaches `main` unchallenged.

## Fix

Add `actionlint` to the existing `lint` job. It bundles shellcheck integration
for `run:` blocks, so one step covers both:

```yaml
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - name: Lint Dockerfile
        uses: hadolint/hadolint-action@2332a7b74a6de0dda2e2221d575162eba76ba5e5 # v3.3.0
        with:
          dockerfile: Dockerfile
      # Runs shellcheck over every `run:` block — which is what the
      # `# shellcheck disable=SC2046` directive in the merge job assumes.
      - name: Lint workflows
        uses: docker://rhysd/actionlint:1.7.12
        with:
          args: -color
```

`verify` already depends on `lint`, so this gates publication with no other
change.

## Resolution
Added a 'Lint workflows' step to the lint job using actionlint pinned by digest (sha256:b1934ee5...), which runs shellcheck over every run: block - the linter the merge job's '# shellcheck disable=SC2046' directive was written for. verify already needs lint, so this gates publication. Verified: actionlint -shellcheck passes on the edited workflow.
title: The workflow carries a shellcheck directive for a linter no CI job runs; the Dockerfile is linted but the pipeline shell is not

body:
## Problem

This assertion is the pipeline's only defence against the exact bug this
repository shipped for its entire history — an empty `XMRIG_VERSION` silently
building master HEAD. `.github/workflows/build.yaml:67-74`:

```bash
expected="$(sed -n 's/^ARG XMRIG_VERSION="v\{0,1\}\([^"]*\)"/\1/p' Dockerfile)"
out="$(docker run --rm xmrig:ci /bin/xmrig --version)"
echo "$out" | grep -q "$expected"
```

`grep -q "$expected"` is an unanchored **regular expression** match against the
whole multi-line output. Two independent weaknesses:

1. **Unescaped metacharacters.** `expected` is `6.22.2`; each `.` matches any
   character, so `6a22b2` satisfies it.
2. **No anchor.** Any substring match anywhere in the output passes, including
   inside the library versions on the following lines.

## Evidence

The real output has three version-bearing lines the pattern may match against:

```
$ docker run --rm xmrig:audit /bin/xmrig --version
XMRig 6.22.2
 built on Aug  2 2026 with GCC 15.2.0
 features: 64-bit AES

libuv/1.52.1
OpenSSL/3.5.7
hwloc/2.12.2
```

Concrete failing scenario: `ARG XMRIG_VERSION="v6.22.2"` while the builder in
fact produces `6.22.21` (an upstream point release, or a stale layer). The
binary prints `XMRig 6.22.21`, `grep -q '6.22.2'` matches the leading substring,
the gate passes, and the image publishes labelled `v6.22.2`. The one check
designed to catch a version mismatch cannot detect a version mismatch in the
direction that actually occurs.

## Impact

A weak assertion on the pipeline's most important gate. The published image
carries `org.opencontainers.image.version` and the NOTICE corresponding-source
pointer, both of which name a version CI did not truly verify.

## Fix

Compare the parsed field for exact equality instead of pattern-matching the blob:

```yaml
      - name: Smoke test
        run: |
          expected="$(sed -n 's/^ARG XMRIG_VERSION="v\{0,1\}\([^"]*\)"/\1/p' Dockerfile)"
          test -n "$expected" || { echo "could not read XMRIG_VERSION from Dockerfile"; exit 1; }
          out="$(docker run --rm xmrig:ci /bin/xmrig --version)"
          echo "$out"
          actual="$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1 == "XMRig" { print $2; exit }')"
          if [ "$actual" != "$expected" ]; then
            echo "::error::built binary is XMRig '${actual}', expected '${expected}' — check the builder-stage ARG"
            exit 1
          fi
```

`awk` pins the field to position 2 of the `XMRig` line, and `[ = ]` is a string
comparison with no regex semantics, so neither weakness survives.

## Resolution
Replaced 'grep -q $expected' with an awk field extraction ($1 == "XMRig" { print $2 }) compared by string equality, so neither the unescaped dots nor the missing anchor survive. Verified both directions on the rebuilt image: the new form gives expected='6.22.2' actual='6.22.2' PASS, and the old grep still matches the string 'XMRig 6.22.21' - confirming the weakness was real, not theoretical.
title: The smoke test asserts the built version with an unanchored, unescaped grep that can pass on the wrong version

## Problem

`README.md:129-135` documents log access with a single command:

```markdown
## Logging

This Docker image sends the container logs to the `stdout`. To view the logs, run:

    docker logs xmrig
```

`docker logs xmrig` resolves the container **name** `xmrig`. That name exists
only for the `docker run` recipe, which sets it explicitly at `README.md:69`:

```bash
    --name xmrig ivuorinen/docker-xmrig:latest
```

Compose does not use it. `docker-compose.yml` declares no `container_name`, so
Compose derives one as `<project>-<service>-<n>` — `docker-xmrig-xmrig-1` for a
clone of this repository, and something else for any other directory name. The
documented command fails with `Error: No such container: xmrig`.

## Evidence

The README presents Compose as a first-class path immediately above this
section (`README.md:74-81`):

```markdown
If you prefer **Docker Compose**, edit the `docker-compose.yml`
manifest as needed and run:

    docker compose up -d
```

A reader who follows that path, then scrolls to Logging, gets a command that
cannot work. There is no `container_name:` key in `docker-compose.yml` to make
it work, and the Kubernetes equivalent two lines further down is given correctly
(`kubectl logs --follow -n xmrig <pod-name>`), so Compose is the one path of
three left without a working command.

## Impact

Minor but certain: the documented command fails for one of the three deployment
methods the README itself recommends, in the section an operator reaches when
something has already gone wrong and they are trying to see why.

## Fix

Give the per-path command, matching how the Kubernetes case is already handled:

```markdown
## Logging

This Docker image sends the container logs to the `stdout`. To view the logs:

```bash

# started with `docker run --name xmrig`

docker logs xmrig

# started with `docker compose up` (Compose names the container

# <project>-xmrig-1, so address it by service name instead)

docker compose logs -f xmrig
```

For Kubernetes run:

```bash
kubectl logs --follow -n xmrig <pod-name>
```
```

## Resolution
The Logging section now gives the command per deployment path: 'docker logs xmrig' for the named docker run, 'docker compose logs -f xmrig' for Compose with a note that Compose names the container <project>-xmrig-1. Confirmed the original defect first: a Compose-started container is xmrigaudit-xmrig-1 and 'docker logs xmrig' returns 'Error response from daemon: No such container: xmrig'.
title: The Logging section gives a docker logs command that does not work for the Compose deployment it sits directly below

body:
## Problem

`README.md:49-51` makes a specific and otherwise careful disclosure about what
leaves the container in cleartext:

> - user: your-miner-identifier. Defaults to `${HOSTNAME}`, which xmrig expands
>   to the container hostname and sends to the pool **in cleartext** — set an
>   explicit value if you do not want that, or enable `tls`.

The `user` field is not the only thing in that packet. The stratum login also
carries an `agent` string identifying the miner version, the libuv version and
the compiler used to build it. Nothing in the repository mentions it, and
`config.json:48` ships the key that controls it — `"user-agent": null` — with
no explanation of what it does.

## Evidence

Captured off the wire from the image built by this repository, pointed at a
listening socket in place of a pool:

```
$ docker run -d --memory 3g -v ./config.json:/etc/xmrig/config.json:ro xmrig:audit
```

The first bytes it sends, unencrypted:

```json
{"id":1,"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"login","params":{
  "login":"6f53695cd88b",
  "pass":"",
  "agent":"XMRig/6.22.2 (Linux x86_64) libuv/1.52.1 gcc/15.2.0",
  "algo":["cn/1","cn/2",...,"rx/0",...,"ghostrider"]}}
```

`login` is the container hostname, exactly as documented — the README's claim is
accurate and was verified. `agent` is the undocumented part:
`XMRig/6.22.2 (Linux x86_64) libuv/1.52.1 gcc/15.2.0`.

That triple — xmrig version, libuv version, compiler version — is close to a
unique identifier for *this image*. Stock XMRig releases are built with a
different toolchain; `gcc/15.2.0` with `libuv/1.52.1` is a fingerprint of the
Alpine 3.24 builder stage at `Dockerfile:8-32`. A pool operator can single out
every deployment of this image, and correlate them across changed `user` values
— which is precisely what a reader who followed the README's advice to "set an
explicit value" believes they have prevented.

## Impact

Incomplete disclosure in the one place the repository chose to be explicit about
cleartext transmission. A reader who sets an explicit `user` to avoid being
identified is still fingerprintable, and the config key that would address it is
present but unexplained.

## Fix

Complete the disclosure and document the existing knob. `README.md:47-53`:

```markdown
- Provide your pool configuration:
  - url: your-p2pool-node:3333 (replace the `CHANGE-ME.example` placeholder)
  - user: your-miner-identifier. Defaults to `${HOSTNAME}`, which xmrig expands
    to the container hostname and sends to the pool **in cleartext** — set an
    explicit value if you do not want that, or set `"tls": true` inside the pool
    object if your pool offers a TLS port.
  - pass: ""

Two other things travel to the pool in the same cleartext login, whatever you
set `user` to:

- `agent` — `XMRig/6.22.2 (Linux x86_64) libuv/1.52.1 gcc/15.2.0`. The version
  triple identifies this image specifically. Override it with the `user-agent`
  key in `config.json` (shipped as `null`, meaning "use the default") if you do
  not want the deployment fingerprinted.
- `algo` — the full list of algorithms this build supports.
```

Add the matching comment beside the key itself so the two do not drift:

```json
  "user-agent": null,
```
→ document in the README's tuning table that `null` means the default agent
string above, and any string replaces it.

## Resolution
The README pool-configuration section now discloses the two other cleartext fields in the stratum login - the agent string (captured verbatim: 'XMRig/6.22.2 (Linux x86_64) libuv/1.52.1 gcc/15.2.0', a version triple that identifies this image specifically) and the algo list - and documents the existing user-agent key in config.json as the override, noting it is shipped as null meaning 'use the default'.
title: The cleartext-disclosure note covers the pool user but not the agent string, which fingerprints the exact image build to the pool operator

## Problem

`.hadolint.yaml` silences DL3018 for the whole Dockerfile and justifies it:

```yaml
ignored:
  # DL3018 wants `apk add pkg=version`. Alpine drops old package versions from the
  # repositories on every refresh, so a pinned apk line breaks the build the first
  # time upstream rebuilds. The base image DIGEST is the pin that holds — a bare
  # `alpine:3.24` tag would not, it is republished on every patch release.
  - DL3018
```

"The base image DIGEST is the pin that holds" is not true of what DL3018 is
about. A digest pins the contents of the base *layer*. `apk add` runs at build
time and fetches from the live Alpine repository, so the package versions it
installs are whatever `dl-cdn.alpinelinux.org` serves that day — entirely
outside the digest's control.

## Evidence

DL3018 fires on two lines, and the comment only reasons about one of them:

```
$ hadolint --config /dev/null Dockerfile
Dockerfile:17 DL3018 warning: Pin versions in apk add...
Dockerfile:50 DL3018 warning: Pin versions in apk add...
```

`Dockerfile:17` is the builder stage — nothing from it is published, so the
argument is sound there. `Dockerfile:50` is the **runtime** stage:

```dockerfile
RUN apk --no-cache add libuv hwloc libssl3 && \
```

Those three, plus their transitive dependencies, are shipped. Today's build
resolved them to:

```
$ syft xmrig:audit -o table
hwloc       2.12.2-r0   apk
libcrypto3  3.5.7-r0    apk
libssl3     3.5.7-r0    apk
libuv       1.52.1-r0   apk
musl        1.2.6-r2    apk
```

Rebuilding the same commit after Alpine publishes 3.24.2 yields different
versions of all of them, with the digest unchanged.

## Impact

The rule is correctly ignored — Alpine really does garbage-collect old package
versions, so pinning them really would break the build. But the stated reason
is wrong in a way that misleads: a reader concludes the runtime stage is
reproducible when it is not, and may skip a `trivy` re-scan of a rebuilt image
on the strength of it.

## Fix

Correct the justification to say what the digest actually covers and what
remains floating:

```yaml
ignored:
  # DL3018 wants `apk add pkg=version`. Alpine garbage-collects old package
  # versions from its repositories, so a pinned apk line breaks the build the
  # first time upstream rebuilds.
  #
  # What this costs: the base LAYER is digest-pinned, but `apk add` fetches from
  # the live repository at build time, so the runtime stage's libuv/hwloc/libssl3
  # (Dockerfile:50) are NOT reproducible across rebuilds of the same commit —
  # they track the 3.24 branch. That is the intended trade: security patches
  # arrive without a Dockerfile edit. It is also why `verify` re-scans the image
  # with trivy on every build rather than trusting a previous scan.
  - DL3018
```

## Resolution
Rewrote the DL3018 justification in .hadolint.yaml to state what the digest actually covers: the base layer is pinned but apk add fetches from the live repository at build time, so the runtime stage's libuv/hwloc/libssl3 are not reproducible across rebuilds of the same commit. The comment now names that as the intended trade and explains that it is why verify re-scans with trivy every run rather than trusting a prior scan.
title: The DL3018 ignore is justified by a claim about digest pinning that does not hold for the runtime stage it also silences

## Problem

None of the five jobs in `.github/workflows/build.yaml` (`lint`, `verify`,
`build`, `merge`, `update_description`) sets `timeout-minutes`. GitHub's default
is 360 minutes per job.

## Evidence

The work these jobs do is bounded and short. The dominant cost is the xmrig
compile, measured locally at:

```
#11 [builder 5/5] RUN cmake .. -DWITH_OPENCL=OFF -DWITH_CUDA=OFF && make -j"$(nproc)"
#11 DONE 106.2s
```

Several minutes on a GitHub-hosted runner; every other step is seconds. A job
that has not finished in ~30 minutes is stuck, not slow.

There are plausible ways to hang: a `docker run` that never exits (the smoke
test at `.github/workflows/build.yaml:69` runs a miner binary), a registry or
Trivy-database fetch that stalls without its own timeout, or a `docker buildx
imagetools create` waiting on Docker Hub. `concurrency.cancel-in-progress`
(`build.yaml:12-14`) does not help — it cancels superseded runs, and each tag
push is its own concurrency group.

## Impact

Informational. A wedged release job can occupy a runner for six hours and delay
or block subsequent runs, and the failure presents as "still running" rather
than as an error. No correctness impact.

## Fix

Add a bound to each job, generous enough never to fire in normal operation:

```yaml
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10

  verify:
    timeout-minutes: 45      # two full xmrig compiles' worth of headroom

  build:
    timeout-minutes: 45

  merge:
    timeout-minutes: 15

  update_description:
    timeout-minutes: 10
```

## Resolution
Added timeout-minutes to all five jobs: lint 10, verify 45, build 45, merge 15, update_description 10. The 45-minute bounds leave roughly two full xmrig compiles of headroom on a hosted runner while cutting the failure mode from six hours to a clear timeout.
title: No job sets timeout-minutes, so any hang in the release pipeline runs against the 360-minute default
